notes.meaning: Jesus and his disciples arrive at the village of Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. From here, Jesus sends two disciples on a specific errand. He chooses this open and public arrival because the time has come for him to suffer and bring salvation.

Jesus instructs the two disciples to go into the next village, where they will find a tied donkey and her young colt. He tells them to untie the animals and bring them to him. This shows his divine knowledge of small details and his gentle power over creation.

Jesus prepares the disciples for any questions by telling them to say, 'The Lord needs them.' He assures them that the owners will let the animals go right away. Even in his humble earthly walk, Jesus acts as the rightful Master who owns and directs all things.

Matthew explains that these actions fulfill ancient words from the prophets Isaiah and Zechariah. The Messiah, God's promised rescuer and King, would not ride a proud war horse like an earthly general, but a gentle donkey. Christ came in peace and humility to offer himself for his people.

The two disciples follow Jesus' directions without arguing or hesitating. They go straight into the village and do exactly what he asked. Their quick obedience shows real trust in their Master, even when the task could have seemed risky or strange.

The disciples bring both the donkey and her colt to Jesus and spread their outer coats over them to serve as a saddle. Jesus then sits on the garments to ride toward Jerusalem. In this simple way, his followers treat him with the honor due to a king.

A large crowd welcomes Jesus by spreading their coats along the dirt road, while others cut branches from nearby trees to lay before him. In the ancient world, people used these actions to welcome a new king or a returning conqueror. The crowds openly show their joy and loyalty to Jesus.

Crowds walking in front of Jesus and behind him shout joyful words from Psalm 118. They cry out 'Hosanna,' which means 'save now,' and call him the Son of David, meaning the promised King from David's family line. God moved the people to give Christ royal praise as he entered the holy city.

The entire city of Jerusalem is shaken with excitement and curiosity as the loud parade enters the gates. The local residents and visiting pilgrims want to know who this honored traveler is. Jesus' public arrival makes it impossible for anyone to ignore him.

The traveling crowd answers that this is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee. A prophet is a messenger who speaks God's truth, and many hoped Jesus was the great prophet promised by Moses. While naming Nazareth pointed to his humble upbringing, honest seekers would soon see he was far more than an ordinary teacher.

Jesus enters the temple courts and drives out the merchants who were buying and selling sacrificial animals. He also knocks over the tables of the money changers, who traded foreign money for temple coins at unfair rates. Jesus exercises his divine right to clean out greedy business from his Father's sacred house.

Jesus quotes the Old Testament prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah to explain his actions. God intended the temple to be a sacred house of prayer for all nations, but dishonest sellers turned it into a hiding place for thieves. God demands that places set apart for worship remain holy and pure.

People who are blind and lame come to Jesus right in the cleared temple courts, and he heals them. Having removed the noisy markets, Jesus turns the temple into a place of divine mercy and help. These miracles offer clear proof that he is the Messiah sent by God.

The leading priests and religious teachers become furious when they see Jesus healing people and hear children shouting praises to the Son of David. Instead of being glad about God's power, they are jealous of Jesus' popularity. Their proud hearts blind them to the good work happening right before their eyes.

The leaders ask Jesus if he hears what the young children are shouting. Jesus answers by quoting Psalm 8, pointing out that God has planned praise to come from the mouths of children and infants. God often receives the purest worship from the small and humble, while proud leaders reject him.

Jesus turns away from the hostile leaders, leaves Jerusalem, and walks about two miles to the quiet village of Bethany. He spends the night there with close friends rather than staying in the city. This became his regular habit during his final week before the cross.

Early the next morning, Jesus heads back toward Jerusalem and feels hungry along the way. This detail reminds readers that Jesus took on a real human body and experienced normal human needs like hunger. He was eager to start his day early so he could teach in the temple.

Jesus notices a fig tree by the road covered with leaves, but when he walks up to it, he finds no fruit at all. He speaks a curse over it, commanding that it never bear fruit again, and the tree dries up at once. This miracle served as a living warning of God's judgment on religious hypocrisy that looks impressive outside but produces no real spiritual fruit.

The disciples are completely astonished when they notice how fast the fig tree died all the way to its roots. They ask how such a healthy-looking tree could dry up so quickly. Jesus' word holds absolute power over nature, and the disciples are still learning to trust that authority.

Jesus tells his disciples that if they have firm faith in God without wavering, they will be able to do even greater things. In Jewish speech, moving a mountain was a common picture for overcoming massive, seemingly impossible problems. He encourages them to rely completely on God's power when facing great difficulties.

Jesus assures the disciples that whatever they ask for in prayer, they will receive if they truly believe. This is not an excuse to ask for selfish wishes, but a promise that God answers prayers prayed with genuine trust in his will. True faith rests fully in God's goodness and power.

When Jesus returns to the temple to teach, the chief priests and respected elders approach him to demand his credentials. They ask who gave him the right to overturn the market and teach the crowds without their permission. Because they cannot deny his miracles, they try to trap him by attacking his official authority.
